claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native, thin iron oxide/hydroxide surface film formed under ambient conditions.
The native film protects Q235 steel against room-temperature corrosion.
The room-temperature passive film self-heals in the presence of environmental moisture and salts.
The native film becomes unstable when Q235 steel is exposed to aggressive salt at 700–900 °C.
High-temperature salt flux acts as an oxidizing catalyst that disrupts the passive film.
Accelerated ionic transport along oxide grain boundaries and defects causes high-temperature film destabilization.
Disruption of the passive film compromises its barrier function and accelerates corrosion.
The relevant surface oxide consists primarily of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3.
The continuity, composition, grain-boundary density, and defect structure of the oxide film mediate corrosion protection.
Oxidizing pre-annealing can thicken or otherwise modify the oxide scale without altering the bulk microstructure.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 will show a greater mass change than room-temperature salt-exposed Q235.
High-temperature salt-exposed Q235 will develop a more porous and discontinuous oxide structure than the room-temperature reference.
High-temperature salt exposure will reduce Q235 hardness as a consequence of accelerated corrosion degradation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to alloyed, deliberately passivated, coated, or stable-crystalline-oxide-scale forms of Q235.
The proposed mechanism is limited to aggressive high-temperature salt-flux environments and may not operate under milder conditions.

contradictions.description: The target is described as Q235 in its as-received state with its native oxide, but the falsification design pre-cleans every specimen. Pre-cleaning can remove or alter the as-received native film, so the tested initial state is not necessarily the one specified by the hypothesis.
